items.article: ‘The day Saff came into the studio with red hair, I said, “We’re gonna be massive!” It was the missing link’ We always had a vision of mixing acid house with indie rock, and we managed to rent a space and build our own studio in London’s Shoreditch area, long before it got trendy. I had a little vocal booth called Hattie Jacques, in honour of the Carry On films but also because it’s Cockney rhyming slang [for shakes]. We spent all our money rewiring it, and that’s where we wrote, recorded and produced Ready to Go – 100 mixes later! We were perfectionists and wanted to do it all ourselves. Every sonic element had to be special up to the point where we ended up arguing. Like at a rave when you stand and dance by the speakers, everything was done with the listener in mind. It was a collaborative effort, but Johnny Male and I wrote most of the song’s lyrics and the melody. We had a really good camaraderie, finishing each other’s sentences, him on an acoustic guitar and me scribbling things down. Tim Dorney and Andy Todd worked more on the technology and synth sounds. We pooled our skills, resources and dreams. The song is all about daily life and things that happened to us. We didn’t write anything too existential – I don’t really like singing about myself – but I’ve always believed in language and the power of the pen. I think it was Johnny who came up with the line, “Ready to go.” It had an anthemic feel and we wanted it to be a bit of a battlecry: “It’s a crack, I’m back!”

items.text: Why Gen Z are planning for life without a state pension
items.article: Many younger people do not believe the state pension will exist when they are older Why Gen Z are planning for life without a state pension Joel has finally landed his first graduate engineering job after several years of lower‑paid roles. He's in his early 20s, lives with his parents and works in London. But instead of splashing the extra cash, or saving up for holidays or a house deposit, he's decided to squirrel more of it away into his workplace pension. The reason? He doesn't think he'll get any kind of state pension. Like Joel, around half of Gen Z (those born from 1997–2012) say they don't expect the state pension to exist by the time they retire. It's pretty stark to hear, but growing up with constant headlines about an ageing population, a proportionally smaller working-age population, and the pressure that government finances are under, Joel thinks it's his generation that will suffer. "I don't believe that I'll be a recipient of a state pension. I know a lot of people my age don't think they're going to be... There just won't be enough money," he says. Retirement has always felt distant when you're in your 20s - something to think about later. But what's emerging among today's under‑30s is something different: not just distance, but doubt. "It just mathematically doesn't make sense… There has to get to a point where that state pension is taking up too much of the budget and can't exist in the way that it exists right now," Joel says.

items.text: Why Burnham’s voting reforms could backfire on Labour
items.article: Andy Burnham has put electoral reform back on the agenda, but could changing Britain’s voting system hand Reform UK an unexpected advantage? Maja Anushka reports Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. A ndy Burnham’s plans for electoral reform could end up boosting Reform UK ’s representation in parliament, former No 10 special adviser Cleo Watson has warned. The prime minister used his Labour Party conference speech to announce a new national commission on electoral reform and invited other parties to take part. He also committed Labour to fighting the next election on a manifesto pledge to change the voting system “so that everyone’s vote counts and everyone’s voice is heard”. Under the UK’s current first-past-the-post system, the candidate with the most votes in each constituency wins the seat. Proportional systems , by contrast, are designed to make the overall distribution of seats more closely reflect parties’ shares of the vote. That could have significant consequences for Westminster. At the 2024 general election, Labour won 411 seats with 33.7 per cent of the vote, while Reform took 14.3 per cent but returned just five MPs. The Liberal Democrats, with 12.2 per cent of the vote, won 72 seats. The Commons Library described the gap between vote share and seat share at that election as the most disproportionate on record.
